transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-17
Start time: 14:30 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood ML Eng), Sanjay Patel (AtlasData Head of ML), Emma Li (AtlasData ML Eng), Omar Hassan (AtlasData Infra), Hannah Brooks (Atlas PM)

Summary (auto): weekly POC sync to review INT8 vs FP8 quantization runs, quality metrics (perplexity, em/rerank), inference perf deltas, and next steps for benchmark/rollout decisions. Some noisy transcription; proper nouns may be off.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: ok hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll give it a few more seconds but want to start on time. this is the weekly quantization sync, maya from redwood, diego and priya on the engineering side.
[00:12] Sanjay: hey Maya, thanks, we have Emma and Omar and Hannah here. quick reminder we're hoping to finalize quant profile recommendation by end of month.
[00:22] Maya: perfect yep that's the goal. Diego do you want to kick off with the latest perf numbers?
[00:28] Diego: sure, I'll share my screen in a sec but quick top-level: we ran the INT8 pipeline across your 1k eval prompts and also tested the new FP8 alpha profile on the same hardware (A100-ish equivalent). numbers: INT8 reduced token compute by about 2.9x on our microbench markers, FP8 was around 3.6x — corresponding to median throughput increases. latency P50 improved ~25% for INT8 and ~35% for FP8, P95 improvements were smaller: ~15% INT8, ~22% FP8. those are with no batching optimizations and without prefix caching.
[01:12] Emma: sorry quick q, what's the difference between this FP8 you're running and the earlier fp8 we tried a few weeks ago? is it the quant scheme or kernel change?
[01:20] Diego: good call, earlier was experimental block-quantization; this FP8 uses dynamic mantissa allocation and a new kernel path that keeps softmax stable. so fewer quality regressions in long-context. but still alpha.
[01:34] Priya: additionally we added per-layer calibration for the attention heads which improves top-k generation metrics; it reduces hallucination on your retrieval examples.
[01:44] Sanjay: can you show the eval deltas — like exact metrics for our reranker and the generation tasks?
[01:50] Diego: yes. so for your reranking benchmark (NDCG@10), baseline FP16 is 0.82. INT8 came in at 0.80 - so tiny regression - and FP8 at 0.815, closer to baseline. for generation F1 we saw INT8 drop maybe 1.8 percentage points on average, FP8 about 0.7 points. perplexity delta: INT8 +3.5%, FP8 +1.1%. i can paste the spreadsheet link after.
[02:20] Hannah: nice, that aligns with what we saw in the initial runs. are those runs with KV cache warm or cold?
[02:27] Diego: cold cache for these numbers. good question. with warm KV cache the latency gaps shrink; effective per-token cost drops further because we avoid recompute on prefix. we'll run a warm-cache pass next.
[02:37] Omar: also curious about batching. our traffic profile is bursty; how stable are perf gains under small batches?
[02:43] Priya: we ran microbench with batch sizes 1,4,8. INT8 gives biggest wins at batch 1 and 4; at batch 8 the relative advantage narrows because kernel saturation hits. FP8 holds up slightly better at larger batch sizes. but the important thing is throughput per GPU hour — FP8 was best in most of our simulated real-world queues.
[03:06] Sanjay: what about end-to-end latency for our user flows — the chat flow with tool-calling? any regressions on model behavior?
[03:14] Diego: tool-calling paths we tested — FP8 preserves the function-calling tokens structure, minimal tokenization errors. there were a couple of corner cases where integer overflow in older kernels caused token probabilities to jitter, but those are fixed in the kernel we ran. still, we flagged a small regression in one prompt with heavy code generation — INT8 failed to close braces properly in one example. FP8 handled it fine.
[03:40] Emma: hmm that code gen issue concerns us; it's part of our app. can you point to the sample?
[03:45] Diego: yes, i have the sample 453 in the sheet — it's the prompt that asks to generate a SQL migration script. with INT8 the model sometimes omits the commit statement; FP8 produced the commit. i'll paste links after.
[03:57] Maya: quick process note — given you're an enterprise customer, we recommend a staged rollout: start with host default route on FP8 for non-critical traffic, keep INT8 for batch jobs, run canary on dedicated nodes. that reduces risk and isolates quality regressions.
[04:15] Sanjay: that makes sense. what's the engineering effort to maintain two profiles?
[04:20] Priya: minimal; the runtime supports multiple quant profiles and runtime switching. there's some ops work to configure routes/policies in the console. Diego, maybe talk about the config?
[04:29] Diego: yeah, from the infra side it's a routing rule: route by tag 'fp8-canary' vs 'int8-batch'; couple of lines in the deployment yaml and policy for rollback. for Dedicated we can pin shards to profile. we also provide a small autoscaling tweak to prefer FP8 if latency SLOs are tight.
[04:45] Omar: on security side, any change? FP8 or INT8 affect encryption/KMS?
[04:50] Maya: no, quantization is model weights/compute — encryption in transit and at rest via KMS unaffected. for private deployments we can ensure HSM integration still covers model artifacts.
[04:59] Sanjay: ok good. can we talk about the quality threshold — like what's the pass/fail criteria?
[05:04] Hannah: we proposed earlier that any profile used in production should have less than 1.5% delta on our primary generation metric and no functional regressions on critical prompts.
[05:12] Sanjay: correct — NDCG drop no more than 0.01 absolute and no critical failures.
[05:17] Priya: from Redwood's side, we recommend FP8 for your chat flows since it meets those thresholds in our runs; INT8 is still great for aggressive cost cuts on background processing.
[05:30] Emma: are there cost numbers — like estimated per-token cost reduction for our mix?
[05:34] Diego: quick back-of-the-envelope: INT8 gave ~2.9x compute reduction, FP8 ~3.6x — but end-to-end cost also depends on latency SLOs, batching, and model sharding. for your traffic we estimate FP8 lowers per-token bill by ~55% vs FP16 on Hosted; INT8 about ~48%. i'll attach a detailed cost model.
[05:58] Sanjay: that's compelling. but we need to validate quality on our internal eval set which includes 200 safety/regulatory prompts.
[06:06] Maya: absolutely, Emma will run those, right?
[06:09] Emma: yes we'll run them this week. one ask — can you provide the docker image tag and the quant config we're using?
[06:14] Diego: sure, current image is redwood/inference:2025-06-10-fp8-alpha. quant config file name qconfig_atlas_v3.json, i'll drop both in the drive.
[06:24] Sanjay: timeline wise — if Emma runs tests and we look good, what would the next step to go to dedicated?
[06:30] Maya: typical flow: pilot on Hosted with canary FP8 for a subset of traffic (we'll set up routes), then move to Dedicated if you want capacity isolation and commit pricing. for Dedicated we can allocate a small shard for your pilot and we can reserve burst capacity. contract timelines depend but engineers can provision a pilot cluster within 2-3 weeks after paperwork.
[06:48] Hannah: any compliance checks for Dedicated? we need SOC2 and audit logs.
[06:52] Maya: yes Dedicated includes audit logs and we support SAML SSO, RBAC, and SOC2 docs — i'll attach the security pack.
[06:58] Omar: also important: can we run the on-prem package in our staging for the FP8 kernel? we want to test in our network environment.
[07:04] Diego: you can — our private deployment supports the same kernels; the only caveat is we need to coordinate driver/kernel versions for the FP8 optimized paths. i'll provide a compatibility matrix.
[07:14] Sanjay: great. any blockers on Redwood's side to run another warm-cache pass and the FP8 cold-to-warm latency sweep?
[07:20] Diego: no blockers. we can run both and share results by Thursday.
[07:24] Maya: let's capture the exact deliverables: diego will run warm-cache + batching sweep; emma will run internal evals including the safety prompts; maya will send pricing and security docs.
[07:34] Sanjay: sounds good. can we also get the sample that failed with INT8? we want to poke at it.
[07:38] Diego: yes sample 453 and sample 612, i'll include both.
[07:42] Emma: also, small ask — can the sheet include per-example perplexity so we can triage ones that jump the most?
[07:47] Priya: yes we'll add per-example metrics in an additional tab and rank by delta.
[07:52] Hannah: on the user-facing side, if we move FP8 to 20% traffic, what's the rollback plan if we see regression?
[07:58] Diego: rollback is immediate via route change; we also set up automatic fallback to FP16 for flagged prompts using prompt hashing — small config.
[08:06] Sanjay: ok good. any conversation about model variants — would you recommend changing model size with quant (e.g., using a slightly smaller FP16 model plus FP8 to get cost vs perf)?
[08:17] Priya: interesting. mixing smaller model + FP8 can get you good economics but increases risk on quality. for your use-case we think staying with the same base model and using FP8 is lower risk. we can test a medium-sized variant if you want.
[08:30] Emma: timeline for the dedicated benchmark?
[08:32] Diego: we'll propose slots next week; prefer mid-week to avoid infra maintenance windows.
[08:37] Maya: okay let's open the Q&A — any other concerns from the team?
[08:42] Omar: operationally, what about monitoring — can Redwood expose per-profile latency/cost dashboards?
[08:47] Maya: yes console exposes per-route per-model breakdowns, token-level cost, and tracing hooks. we'll enable a dashboard for your account.
[08:55] Sanjay: what about regressions that only show up in long context (8k+) — did you test long context cases?
[09:00] Diego: we ran 8k token tests; FP8 maintained stability thanks to dynamic mantissa; INT8 had more variance beyond 6k. i'll include that in the report.
[09:10] Emma: can you also include the kernel versions and CUDA driver used? we need to match them in staging.
[09:15] Diego: sure: CUDA 12.2, driver 550.xx, kernel path v2.4.3-fp8.
[09:21] Hannah: good. i'd like a short recap at the end with owners.
[09:24] Maya: yup we'll do that.
[09:26] --- long pause while Diego shares screen ---
[12:05] Diego: ok i'm scrolling the spreadsheet — here's the NDCG table and the per-prompt deltas. see the SQL sample at row 453, you can see token-level probs drop around token 42.
[12:18] Emma: saw it, thanks. looks like INT8 truncation around the commit token.
[12:22] Diego: yes slight numeric underflow in that kernel; we patched it but older nodes may still be affected.
[12:28] Sanjay: how about the warm-cache P95 numbers?
[12:31] Diego: warm-cache P95 for FP16 210ms, INT8 185ms, FP8 165ms on our test rig. that's with small batching and the runtime's KV caching enabled.
[12:44] Priya: and cost model summary — per-token cost reduction relative to FP16: INT8 48%, FP8 55% (hosted). for dedicated it's slightly better due to packing.
[12:58] Sanjay: ok good. any security concerns flagged in the safety prompts?
[13:02] Emma: preliminary glance looks fine; a couple of safety prompts show small changes in refusal rates but nothing critical. we'll share full details.
[13:10] Maya: great. let's do a quick product note — we recommend FP8 for production canary, INT8 for batch; pin Dedicated shards if you need isolation. Priya, anything to add?
[13:20] Priya: just that we'll add per-example delta and kernel compatibility notes in the doc.
[13:25] Sanjay: thanks everyone. final ask — would Redwood include a few demo logs for the private deployment so our infra team can sanity check?
[13:32] Diego: yes i'll provide logs and a compatibility matrix.
[13:36] Maya: awesome. ok recap: action items are diego running warm-cache + batch sweep by Thu (2025-06-19), emma to run internal eval incl safety by Tue (2025-06-24), maya to share pricing and security docs by Fri (2025-06-20). we'll reconvene next week same time.
[13:55] Sanjay: thanks all, talk soon.
[14:00] Meeting end.
